To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the permeability of a fractured rock mass can be predicted from ultrasonic velocity anisotropy, provided the orientation distribution of the fractures is known.

(1) the velocity anisotropy of fractured rock can be inverted into an estimate of crack orientation distribution; (2) the permeability anisotropy can be estimated from this orientation information; (3) this permeability model is consistent with existing theories of permeability of fractured rock; (4) permeability estimates are sensitive to the aspect ratio distribution of cracks; (5) permeability estimates can be used to estimate permeability of a fractured rock system from velocity measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an approach to estimate the probability distribution of crack orientation and the permeability of fractured rock from velocity anisotropy.
the development of an integrated methodology for predicting the anisotropic hydraulic properties of fractured rock systems.
the development of an approach to estimate the permeability of fractured rock from the velocity anisotropy observed in ultrasonic measurements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the velocity anisotropy method is a promising approach to estimating permeability of a fractured rock, but that further work on the modeling of permeability is required.
the velocity measurements and inversion for the crack distribution function are good and that the permeability model needs further refinement.
this method of estimating permeability from velocity anisotropy is not yet fully developed.

we have developed a methodology that allows the estimation of the anistropic permeability of fractured rock systems from ultrasonic velocities and a knowledge of the uniaxially prestressed fracture distribution.
the velocity inversion method is a powerful tool in estimating the crack density distribution and that the permeability predictions based on these distributions are promising.
the permeability of fractured rock is not a scalar quantity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the velocity inversion for crack orientations provides a powerful tool for predicting permeability in fractured rocks.
ultrasonic velocity measurements can provide information on the fracture distribution in a rock sample, and that this information can then be used to estimate the permeability.
the velocity anisotropy in a uniaxially stressed rock can be used to estimate the anisotropic fracture permeability.
